conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who works with new moms on the emotional ups and downs that can come after baby arrives. Today I’d like to do a quick check-in using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s just 10 short questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days; it helps us spot things like depression or anxiety early so we can get you the right support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone’s in danger. We’ll take it one question at a time, no rush, and you can ask me to pause or clarify anything. Ready to start?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

I can still laugh sometimes—like when my husband makes a goofy face at the baby—but it doesn’t come as easily as it used to. Maybe once or twice in the past week I actually felt a real laugh instead of just forcing a smile.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I can laugh—like if the baby makes a funny sound or my husband jokes around—but it feels kind of muted. I’ll chuckle, but then the happy feeling fades fast and I’m back to feeling flat. Maybe a couple of times in the past week I actually laughed without thinking about it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee or when my mom comes over to hold the baby so I can take a shower—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. I’ll think “that’ll be nice,” rather than really counting down the minutes. Most days it’s just okay, not joyful.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday the baby was fussy for an hour and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or that I’m just not reading her cues right. My head knows it’s probably normal baby stuff, but I still catch myself wondering what I did wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Mostly I feel pretty calm, but a couple of nights I caught myself lying in bed imagining the baby’s breathing had changed or picturing her spitting up and choking. Nothing was actually wrong, yet my stomach still tightened for a few minutes until I peeked in the bassinet and saw she was fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I haven’t had any full panic moments, but once or twice—like when I was at the grocery checkout and the baby started to cry—I felt my heart race and this sudden wave of “I need to get out of here right now.” It passed after a minute, but it left me a little shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah. Like when the laundry pile looks bigger than the baby and she won’t nap unless she’s on me, I feel this tightness in my chest and think, “How am I going to keep doing this every day?” I manage to get through it, but it feels heavier than I expected.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not really. I’m tired and a little down sometimes, but once I finally lie down I drift off pretty fast. Maybe once this week I lay there replaying the day and worrying I’d wake the baby if I moved, so it took an extra half hour, but that was it.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the time—like a heaviness that shows up out of nowhere while I’m folding onesies or feeding her. It’s not every moment; I still smile at the baby and talk to her, but at least a couple of times a day I feel that dull ache in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I cried twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t settle after a feeding and I felt like my body wasn’t doing what it’s “supposed” to do, and once yesterday when my partner asked how I was doing and I just got this sudden wave of sadness and the tears came before I could stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that has crossed my mind—just the opposite; I keep worrying I’m not doing enough to keep her safe and healthy.

Thank you for sharing so openly about these first demanding weeks with your baby. It sounds as though moments of joy are slipping in, yet you're often carrying a persistent <sym>heaviness</sym>, self-doubt, and worry that feel heavier than you expected. Your wish to keep your little one safe shines through, and it's understandable that the day-to-day uncertainties of new motherhood can feel overwhelming.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 15, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only occasional, muted laughter with quick return to flat mood, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>She still finds some mild pleasure but describes a clear reduction from her baseline, matching "definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated self-blame incidents this week, aligning with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports specific, recurring nighttime worries about the baby's safety without objective cause, matching 'Yes, sometimes.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense anxiety/panic symptoms (racing heart, urge to flee) triggered by baby crying, consistent with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports recurring moments of feeling overwhelmed, chest tension, and doubts about sustaining daily tasks, aligning with 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness "a couple of times a day," matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 15 places you above the 14-point cutoff that signals probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed frequent <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>diminished enjoyment</sym>, <sym>tearfulness</sym>, and repeated <sym>self-blame</sym> over infant care, meeting several <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. You also described <sym>panic-like symptoms</sym> (racing heart, urge to flee) and near-daily worries about the baby's safety, indicating co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. No self-harm thoughts were reported. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full evaluation and treatment planning
3. Share your EPDS responses with your provider so they can track progress
4. Continue leaning on your support system; let trusted helpers handle chores so you can rest
5. Practice brief <med>breathing or grounding exercises</med> when you feel chest tightness or panic rising
6. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and anxiety episodes to bring to your next appointment
7. Re-screen with EPDS in 1-2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 15: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (approx. 1–2 wks post-delivery)  
Instrument: EPDS-style 10-item self-report  
Date: ___________

Symptoms endorsed  
- Anhedonia: diminished pleasure/enthusiasm for usual activities (Q1, Q2)  
- Low mood: daily “heaviness,” tearfulness ≥ 2 episodes this week (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame / inappropriate guilt over infant care (Q3)  
- Free-floating anxiety & situational panic symptoms (heart racing, urge to flee) without objective trigger (Q4, Q5)  
- Feeling overwhelmed / unable to manage daily tasks (Q6)  
- Worries focused on infant safety (breathing, choking) (Q4)

Sleep / coping  
- Occasional prolonged sleep-onset secondary to intrusive worries; most nights able to sleep when infant settles (Q7)

Safety  
- Denies suicidal or self-harm ideation (Q10)

Risk pattern  
Persistent mild–moderate depressive symptoms (low mood, anhedonia, crying, guilt) plus sub-threshold anxiety/panic; functional impact evident in “heavier than expected” daily burden; no current safety concerns.

Screening impression  
Elevated score range for both depressive and anxiety factors; findings consistent with probable postpartum depression with anxious features. Recommend formal clinical interview (DSM-5-TR criteria) and consideration of structured follow-up within 1–2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory, coping, and infant–parent functioning.
